clinical_knowledge.topic: Basal Cell Carcinoma evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Basal Cell Carcinoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes biopsy confirmation followed by Mohs micrographic surgery given the high-risk nasal location, with staged reconstruction anticipated for larger defects, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: slowly enlarging pearly nodule with telangiectasias on the nasal tip
Key HPI features: 67M presenting with a slowly enlarging, pearly, translucent nodule with overlying telangiectasias on the nasal tip, with occasional bleeding and crusting.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. 8mm pearly, translucent, dome-shaped nodule on the nasal tip with overlying telangiectasias and fine central crusting, friable with minor trauma. Rolled, well-defined border. No palpable regional lymphadenopathy. No facial numbness, pain, or other signs of perineural invasion.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Basal Cell Carcinoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Squamous cell carcinoma without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Central ulceration (rodent ulcer).
management_principles: Confirm the diagnosis with a shave or punch biopsy before definitive treatment
Refer for Mohs micrographic surgery given the high-risk central facial (nasal) location, for margin control and maximal tissue conservation

Counsel that a full-thickness nasal tip/alar defect after excision may require staged reconstruction (e.g., paramedian forehead flap with structural cartilage grafting and lining), depending on final defect size
Screen for perineural invasion signs (facial numbness, pain, paresthesia) and arrange long-term surveillance given recurrence and new-lesion risk.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 67M presenting with a slowly enlarging, pearly, translucent nodule with overlying telangiectasias on the nasal tip, with occasional bleeding and crusting.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. 8mm pearly, translucent, dome-shaped nodule on the nasal tip with overlying telangiectasias and fine central crusting, friable with minor trauma. Rolled, well-defined border. No palpable regional lymphadenopathy. No signs of perineural invasion.
reference_soap.assessment: Nasal tip nodule with classic pearly, telangiectatic features highly suggestive of basal cell carcinoma, pending confirmatory biopsy.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm with a shave or punch biopsy. If confirmed as BCC, refer for Mohs micrographic surgery given the high-risk nasal location. Counsel the patient that a full-thickness defect at the nasal alar/tip junction after excision may require staged reconstruction (e.g., paramedian forehead flap with cartilage grafting and lining) depending on defect size, and arrange surveillance for recurrence and new lesions.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Basal Cell Carcinoma Nasal Tip Flap Reconstruction

Select the appropriate biopsy technique and surgical approach (Mohs micrographic surgery) for a high-risk facial basal cell carcinoma
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: Most common non-melanoma skin cancer presenting as a translucent, pearly papule with telangiectasias.

must_ask.say: Did this skin bump start as a smooth pearly nodule with visible tiny blood vessels?
Does the lesion bleed easily when touched or develop a central crust that doesn't heal?
Do you have a history of significant sun exposure or outdoor work?
How slowly has this lesion expanded over recent time?
Have you ever had skin cancers or precancerous spots removed before?
